extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, taxonomists, naturalists, and field collectors interested in Indian freshwater invertebrates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for producing a regional faunal monograph (freshwater sponges, hydroids, and polyzoa): scope, structure, nomenclatural practice, geographical treatment, and field/collection notes. Intended to standardize how species, localities, and biological observations are recorded and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: include freshwater representatives; brackish selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the freshwater representatives of the three groups (sponges, coelenterates, polyzoa) in one volume; include brackish forms only where biologically convenient or where they occur in stagnant brackish pools connected with estuaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial scope decision: although primarily Indian freshwater forms are treated, include related brackish-water species when relevant to understanding transitions and local faunas. The author states he at first proposed to include all stagnant-water forms but limited scope for tractability; instead, each part's introduction contains a list of species found in stagnant brackish water with notes and references. Use biological relevance (e.g., occurrence in estuarine pools, evidence of modification) to decide inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical framework: use physiographical regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the geographical list on Col. Alcock and accept, with slight modifications, Blanford's physiographical rather than zoogeographical regions for India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the limits of distribution for aquatic invertebrates depend on different factors than vertebrates; therefore use physiographical regions (physical geography) as the primary regional units. Apply these regions consistently when compiling distribution lists (e.g., Western Frontier Territory, Western Himalayan Territory, Malabar Zone, Indo-Gangetic Plain, etc.). Cite the system used and note any modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of varieties/subspecific ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties are ignored in the geographical list because they are not considered to have a geographical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not list varietal names in the primary geographical distribution lists. Focus on species and subspecies (where appropriate) that have demonstrable geographical importance. If varieties are discussed elsewhere, explain why they were excluded from the distribution list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legend / distribution-symbol convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symbols in the geographical list to indicate broader distributional affinities: '*' indicates species/subspecies only found in one physiographical region; '!' indicates species also found in Europe; '$' in North America; '+' in Africa; '@' in the Malay Archipelago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a clear legend at the start of the geographical list explaining symbol meanings. Apply symbols consistently to every taxon entry to summarise extra-Indian/cosmopolitan affinities at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monograph structure and required components
rubrics_metrics.description: Each part of the volume should include an introduction, glossary of technical terms used in the part, systematic list of taxa, and supporting material such as synopses of classification, explanations of plates, and an appendix (e.g., hints on preparation of specimens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize each taxonomic part with: (1) general introduction (biology, structure, reproduction, distribution, history, bibliography), (2) glossary of technical terms used in that part, (3) systematic list with authorities and page references, (4) synopses of classification and leading characters, (5) plates/explanations and an appendix with practical notes (e.g., specimen preparation). This standardizes presentation and supports both specialists and field workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal/life-history categorization of species
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify species according to seasonal biology (e.g., species that produce resting bodies and flourish in winter; species that flourish mainly during the rains; species that flourish throughout the year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile and present lists of taxa grouped by their phenology (e.g., 'flourish in winter', 'flourish during the rains', 'throughout the year'), with examples and discussion of adaptive/biological significance (e.g., production of gemmules, statoblasts, resting-buds, or hard-shelled eggs). Use observed seasonal occurrence and known reproductive/resting structures as the basis for categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and annotation of brackish-water taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: Give in the introduction to each part a list of species found in stagnant brackish water with a few notes and references to descriptions, rather than attempting to treat all brackish-water fauna in full within the freshwater volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When brackish-water taxa are relevant (especially near estuaries), provide concise annotations and bibliographic references in the part introductions. Avoid expanding the monograph's scope to cover the entire brackish-water fauna; instead, document only those forms that bear on freshwater distributions or that occur in local stagnant brackish pools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field/collecting locality criteria and specimen-habitat notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess collecting localities by features favourable to sponge/polyzoan growth; e.g., tanks/ponds with light and shade, solid supports, prolific aquatic vegetation, sufficient depth, and vicinity to human dwellings favour sponges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting localities, include habitat descriptors that explain species abundance (solid objects for attachment, aquatic plants, depth profiles, degree of siltiness, tidal influence). Note places that are poor collecting grounds (e.g., turbid, silt-laden rivers) and those that are especially productive (e.g., museum tanks). Such details inform sampling strategy and interpret distribution records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altitude and range reporting practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Report altitudinal records for species and note limits of known altitude occurrences (e.g., 'No sponge has been found in Indian territory at an altitude higher than that of Bhim Tal (4,500 feet)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise altitude information where available; highlight limits and gaps in knowledge (regions poorly known, highest/lowest recorded occurrences). Use altitude data to discuss biogeographical and ecological patterns and to identify poorly surveyed regions requiring further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclatural/systematic presentation and index conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a systematic index listing orders, families, genera, subgenera and species with authorship and page references; include synopses of higher-level classification and leading characters of divisions; addenda and glossary entries where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent taxonomic formatting (taxon followed by authority, subspecific notation where used, and page numbers). Include synopses summarising leading characters of divisions or suborders for quick identification. Provide addenda for later corrections and a glossary of technical terms to aid non-specialist readers. When drawing on prior catalogues/lists, state the model/reference used.
